Please read this carefully:

<document>
# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
This is a much stronger study than the Halden pilot. It has a control group, stratified randomisation, a registered protocol, output taken from administrative systems, and actual hours from timesheets. It also fixes most of the problems I raised with the previous paper. Its central distinction, between work tied to presence and work that is not, also explains the pattern the Halden paper overlooked: reversions were concentrated in retail and healthcare administration.

The arithmetic checks out. The remaining issues are mainly about inference and incomplete reporting.

## Arithmetic checks

- **Hours:** 37.9 → 33.0 is −12.9%, and 37.6 → 31.2 is −17.0%.
- **Case-processing per-hour gain:** 0.979 / 0.87 = 1.125, or +12.5%.
- **Counter per-hour gain:** 0.886 / 0.83 = 1.067, or +6.7%.
- **Scheduled-hours version:** 0.979 / 0.80 = 1.224, matching the stated 22%.
- **Per-hour confidence intervals:** dividing the output CIs by the hours ratio gives about +7.1 to +17.9 and +0.1 to +13.4. These are close to the reported intervals. The reported counter interval is slightly *narrower* at the lower end, though, even though uncertainty in hours should widen it. The methods should say how the per-hour intervals were estimated. The hours changes themselves are reported without intervals.

## 1. Inference with few clusters

There are 7 v 7 offices in one stratum and 5 v 5 in the other. Conventional cluster-robust standard errors are known to be too small with this few clusters.

The counter interval (−16.9 to −5.9) looks narrow for 10 offices. The registered analysis should use one of the following, or show that the conclusions survive under them:

- randomisation inference (permutation within strata),
- a wild cluster bootstrap, or
- small-sample-corrected standard errors with t(G−1) critical values.

## 2. Demand spillover between offices

Randomising at office level prevents contamination between colleagues. It does not prevent contamination through the *public*.

If callers or visitors who face longer waits at treated counters go to control offices or other channels, then:
- control output rises,
- treated output falls, and
- the difference-in-differences estimate overstates the effect.

There is a sign of this in the numbers. Abandoned calls rose by only 4 percentage points (6% → 10%), but contacts handled fell by 11.4%. Unless demand fell, about 7% of contacts went somewhere. The paper should report demand at control offices, and the routing rules, so readers can see where that 7% went.

The same question applies, more weakly, to case processing if cases can be reallocated between offices.

## 3. Outcomes registered but not fully reported

**Waiting time** is a registered secondary outcome. It is reported only as treated offices before and after (4.2 → 6.9 minutes), with no control comparison or interval. This is the same before–after design the paper criticises elsewhere.

**Abandoned calls** (6% → 10%) appear only in the text. They are not in the registered outcome list and have no control comparison. They should be labelled as unregistered.

**Quality** is reported as "3.1% v 3.0%" and "11.8% v 10.9%," with no difference-in-differences or intervals. It is also unclear whether these are treated versus control at month 9.

**The counter quality result goes uncommented.** The repeat-contact rate is about 0.9 points higher in treated counter offices. The text discusses quality only for case processing. If the difference is real, service worsened on two dimensions, not one.

**Timeliness in case processing** is not reported, even though the limitations raise the risk of backlogs building beyond statutory deadlines. Cases closed is a throughput measure. It cannot detect:
- easy cases being prioritised,
- the age of the backlog rising, or
- deadline breaches.

Time-to-decision and the share of cases near or past the deadline should be reported. They may already be in the case-management system.

## 4. Hours measurement

**Unclaimed overtime is missed.** Timesheets record overtime that was *claimed*. Unclaimed work, such as work done at home or salaried staff not filing claims, is not captured. Actual hours are therefore a lower bound on hours worked, and the per-hour gains are upper bounds. The limitations should say this.

**The definition of FTE is unclear.** If FTE is defined against 37.5 hours, a treated employee working 30 scheduled hours counts as 0.8 FTE, which would change what "output per FTE" means. The paper appears to mean per headcount-equivalent employee, and should say so explicitly.

## 5. Cost

The county asked whether the schedule could be extended "without loss of service," but cost is a natural follow-up question.

Case-processing staff claimed roughly 3 hours a week of overtime to clear backlogs. If overtime is paid at a premium, the cost per case closed may have *risen* even though output per employee held. Cost per unit of output would make the policy implication much clearer than output per hour does.

## 6. Sick days

**Part of the fall may be mechanical.** The difference-in-differences design removes seasonality, which is an improvement on the Halden pilot. But if the 30-hour rota means fewer working days, there are fewer days on which absence can be recorded. Sick days per scheduled day, or sickness hours as a share of scheduled hours, would separate a mechanical effect from a real health effect.

**Reporting is thin.** The figure is pooled across strata, with no interval and no per-stratum breakdown.

**Resignations** are annualised from nine months, and the imprecision is acknowledged. An interval would still help.

## 7. The exploratory meetings analysis

The caveats are appropriate. A few points would strengthen or qualify the analysis.

**There is no baseline.** Meetings were measured only in month six, so the 3.3-hour gap could partly predate the trial. With 7 v 7 offices, randomisation doesn't guarantee balance.

**The correlation is very uncertain.** For r = 0.71 with n = 7, the 95% interval runs from roughly zero to about 0.95.

**The forking path is visible.** The data were collected because managers requested them. They are reported for case processing only, and counter offices go unmentioned.

**The paper's own figures imply a striking result.** Subtract meeting time from actual hours:

| | Actual hours | Meeting hours | Non-meeting hours |
|---|---|---|---|
| Treated | 33.0 | 3.8 | 29.2 |
| Control | ~37.9 | 7.1 | ~30.8 |

On this rough basis, non-meeting hours fell only about 5% while output fell about 2%. That implies a gain per *non-meeting* hour of only about 3%. If the meeting figures hold up, nearly all of the 12.5% per-hour gain would come from removing meeting time rather than from rest. That is a stronger version of the authors' hypothesis and worth flagging for the 24-month confirmatory test. It rests on the unbaselined month-six data, so it is suggestive only.

## 8. Wording

**"Little or no measurable loss of output per employee"** in the first conclusion is fair for the point estimate. However, the interval cannot rule out a loss of nearly 7%. "Could not detect a loss, and can rule out losses larger than about 7%" is more precise.

**The second conclusion is the paper's most useful contribution.** It separates productivity per hour from productivity per employee, and notes that these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work. It could be moved into the Summary.

**The limitations section is missing items:**
- few-cluster inference,
- demand spillover,
- unclaimed hours,
- unreported timeliness, and
- the multiple secondary outcomes tested without adjustment.

**A baseline balance table** by stratum (staff numbers, pre-period output, hours) would help readers judge the randomisation, given the small number of offices.

## Overall

The registered results support the authors' main conclusions:
- When work is not tied to presence, actual hours fall less than scheduled hours and output per employee is roughly maintained.
- When work is tied to presence, a cut in hours costs output and service, even though each hour worked is more productive.
- Productivity computed against scheduled hours is substantially overstated.

The most important additions would be few-cluster-robust inference, a check for displaced demand, and difference-in-differences estimates for wait times, quality and timeliness.

If useful, I could draft a revised results table with the missing comparisons laid out, or write a short comparison of this trial with the Halden pilot.
